Charleston by the numbers

Where is Charleston and how is the city laid out?

Charleston sits on Charleston Harbor, where the Ashley, Cooper and Wando rivers meet, just south of the middle of South Carolina's coastline. It is the state's most populous city and the seat of Charleston County.

The city covers 135.51 square miles, of which 115.03 is land and 20.48 is water. It reaches into two counties, Charleston and Berkeley, which matters for a seller because the county decides which assessor and treasurer you deal with.

Wikipedia describes six city districts: Downtown (the peninsula between the Ashley and Cooper), West Ashley, Johns Island, James Island, the Cainhoy Peninsula and Daniel Island. A peninsula house and a Johns Island house can sit in the same city but face different flood exposure, parking rules and rental rules.

What is the short history of Charleston?

English colonists founded the settlement as Charles Town in 1670 at Albemarle Point and moved it to its present site in 1680. The city was incorporated on August 13, 1783, and the spelling "Charleston" soon became standard.

The Civil War began in Charleston Harbor with the shelling of Fort Sumter in 1861.

How big is Charleston and what drives its economy?

The 2020 census counted 150,227 residents, up from 120,083 in 2010 and 96,650 in 2000. The 2025 estimate is 159,423, and the three-county metro area (Charleston, Berkeley and Dorchester) had 849,417 people in 2020.

Wikipedia lists tourism, the port, logistics, aerospace and information technology as the economic base. The Port of Charleston is one of the busiest in the country, Boeing has an aerospace presence, and the tech sector has earned the nickname "Silicon Harbor." The College of Charleston and The Citadel are the two colleges named for the city.

City population, 2020 census150,227Wikipedia
City population, 2025 estimate159,423Wikipedia
Total area135.51 square milesWikipedia
Parcels the county assessor appraisesabout 190,000 real property parcelsCharleston County Assessor
Elevation of the city3 feetWikipedia

What does Charleston's climate mean for a house?

The climate is humid subtropical, with mild winters, hot humid summers and rain all year. Average annual precipitation is about 52.5 inches at the airport and 44.3 inches downtown, and nearly half of it falls from June through September.

Hurricanes are the big risk. Hurricane Hugo, a Category 4 storm, struck on September 21, 1989, and caused more than $2.8 billion in damage. Storm history is worth gathering before you list: repair records, roof age and any past water damage.

  • Average relative humidity at the airport is 72.7%.
  • The record airport high is 105 degrees Fahrenheit (August 1, 1999) and the record low is 6 degrees (January 21, 1985).
  • Rain falls in every season, with summer the wettest.

How does flooding affect selling a house in Charleston?

Flooding is a routine part of the sale conversation in Charleston, because the city sits at about 3 feet of elevation. The city's floodplain page lists the Stono, Ashley, Cooper and Wando rivers, several creeks and the Atlantic Ocean as flood sources.

The same page says a property outside the FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area can still have local drainage trouble, unmapped floodplain or sea level rise. The city issues a Flood Hazard Information Letter that shows a property's flood zone, and elevation certificates and flood hazard information can be requested from floodplain-info@charleston-sc.gov. Its 2019 Flooding and Sea Level Rise Strategy recommends planning for 2.0 to 3.0 feet of sea level rise over the next 50 years.

An owner who thinks the FEMA map is wrong can file a Letter of Map Change with FEMA, for example when the lot sits above the Base Flood Elevation or has been filled. Read more on the city's Floodplain Mapping page. The page notes that an elevation certificate sent with a map request can be flagged for compliance problems such as inadequate flood openings in a garage enclosure.

Who bills Charleston property tax and when is it due?

The Charleston County Assessor values the property and the Charleston County Treasurer bills and collects it. Real estate tax is due January 15 of the following year without penalty.

The Treasurer's page sets the late schedule: 3% after January 15, another 7% after February 1 (10% total), and another 5% after March 17 (15% total). After March 17 the bill goes to the Delinquent Tax Department. State law backs this schedule, and a U.S. postmark decides whether a mailed payment was on time (S.C. Code 12-45-180).

StepDate or amount
Tax due without penaltyJanuary 15
First penalty3% after January 15
Second penaltyAdditional 7% after February 1
Third penaltyAdditional 5% after March 17, then to Delinquent Tax

The Treasurer does not accept partial payments, because state law does not allow them. Online payment carries a surcharge. The office is at 101 Meeting St., Suite 120, Charleston, SC 29401, and the phone is (843) 958-4360. The page does not describe how taxes are handled at a closing, so ask the Treasurer or your title company.

How does the Charleston County reassessment work?

South Carolina reassesses every five years, and Charleston County's most recent notices were mailed August 20, 2025. The Assessor says it appraises about 190,000 real property parcels and 6,500 titled mobile homes.

When market value rises more than 15%, the taxable value increase is capped at 15% over the prior value. The page adds that the cap does not limit the tax amount, since millage can change. Newly added property, property with 2024 construction, and property with a 2024 Assessable Transfer of Interest may be uncapped or only partly capped.

  • Appeals must be in writing with an original signature, sent to the Assessor.
  • The objection deadline is 90 days after notices are mailed, and the printed deadline on the 2025 notices was November 18, 2025.
  • If no notice was sent that year, the appeal period generally closes on the tax due date, typically January 15.
  • Later stages have 30-day deadlines, and filing an appeal does not delay the bill.

The Assessor's office is at 4050 Bridge View Dr., Suite 100, North Charleston, SC 29405, phone (843) 958-4100.

What is the 4% legal residence rate and what happens when the owner moves?

Owner-occupied homes are taxed at 4% of fair market value, other real property at 6%, and the 4% rate is not automatic. Under S.C. Code 12-43-220, the owner must have owned and occupied the home as a legal residence and be domiciled there.

Charleston County's Assessor says properties without approval are billed at 6%, and bills show "QR4" when the 4% rate applies. The application deadline is typically January 15. The statute also says the home may not be rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year, and an owner who loses eligibility must tell the assessor within six months or face a penalty of 100% of the tax paid plus interest.

That matters to sellers who moved out before listing. If the house has sat as a rental or vacant, the 6% rate can apply, and your payoff figure at closing will be higher than you expect.

What are the short-term rental rules in the city of Charleston?

The city sorts short-term rentals into categories, and each allows at most one STR unit per property. Category 1 is the Old and Historic District, Category 2 is the rest of the peninsula, and Category 3 covers Daniel Island, James Island, Johns Island and West Ashley.

  • Each category needs one extra off-street parking space beyond the two the zoning ordinance requires per dwelling unit.
  • Category 1 needs a structure individually listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
  • Category 2 needs a building constructed at least 50 years ago.

For eligibility, the city points owners to its property eligibility quiz or shorttermrental@charleston-sc.gov (city category page). A seller who is advertising a house as an investment with STR income should confirm the permit status in writing, since the permit rules depend on location.

What does selling a house with tax due look like in Charleston?

A seller who owes Charleston property tax can sell, and the unpaid amount is normally settled from the sale proceeds at closing. Request a payoff figure from the Treasurer's Office before you sign, since penalties step up on February 1 and March 17.

The Assessor's page confirms that refunds for overpaid taxes may be requested for up to two years, which can help a seller who paid at 6% while eligible for 4%. If you refinanced, the Treasurer reminds owners to send the bill to the mortgage holder so escrow pays it.

We did not find a Charleston County page we could open that explains delinquent tax sale dates, so ask the Delinquent Tax Division directly if a sale notice has arrived.

More questions about Charleston, SC Property Tax Guide

When is Charleston County property tax due?

January 15 of the following year is the last day without penalty, per the Charleston County Treasurer. A 3% penalty applies after that date, then a further 7% after February 1 and 5% after March 17.

How long do I have to appeal my Charleston assessment?

You have 90 days after the notice is mailed to send a written objection to the Assessor, with an original signature. The 2025 notices printed November 18, 2025 as the deadline. Phone, email and fax do not preserve your rights.

Is Charleston in more than one county?

Yes. The city spans Charleston and Berkeley counties, according to Wikipedia. Which county office you deal with depends on where the parcel sits, so check your tax bill before calling.

Can I sell my Charleston house if I owe back property tax?

Yes, and the unpaid tax is typically paid from the proceeds at closing. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure first, because the 10% and 15% penalty totals begin after February 1 and March 17.

Does Charleston have a flood-zone disclosure tool?

The city issues a Flood Hazard Information Letter showing a property's flood zone. Requests for elevation certificates and flood hazard information go to floodplain-info@charleston-sc.gov.

Greenville by the numbers

Where is the city of Greenville, and how big is it?

Greenville is the county seat of Greenville County in the South Carolina Upstate, about halfway between Atlanta and Charlotte along Interstate 85. Columbia, the state capital, is roughly 100 miles to the southeast.

The city covers 30.02 square miles at an elevation of about 955 feet. The Reedy River, a tributary of the Saluda, runs through the center of town. The 2020 Census counted 70,720 people, and the 2025 estimate is 75,310, up from 58,409 in 2010.

Census yearPopulation
195058,161
198058,242
200056,002
201058,409
202070,720

The city lost people for decades, then grew fast after 2010. A house owner who bought in the 1990s has often seen a lot of change on the block, which is one reason many Greenville sellers get calls from investors.

How did Greenville start, and what is its mill history?

Greenville began in 1797 as the village of Pleasantburg, took the name Greenville in 1821, and became a city when the charter was amended in February 1869. Cotton mills and rail lines drove its growth, and by 1915 it was known as the "Textile Center of the South."

Up to 19 mills operated here at one point. Falls Park on the Reedy, dedicated in 2004 at a cost of $15.0 million, now sits where the city began.

The mill era left behind worker cottages, brick commercial blocks and older bungalows. Those older houses often need roof, wiring or plumbing work, and that is the type of property a buyer who pays cash and buys as-is can take without asking you to fix anything.

What companies and schools anchor Greenville's economy?

Michelin moved its North American headquarters to Greenville in 1984, and the city is also home to North American headquarters for Synnex, United Community Bank, AVX, Sage Automotive Interiors, Prisma Health and ScanSource. Bon Secours and Duke Energy are other large employers with offices here.

At the former Donaldson Air Force Base, now the SC Technology and Aviation Center, Lockheed Martin produces the F-16.

  • Bob Jones University and Greenville Technical College are inside city limits.
  • The University of South Carolina School of Medicine Greenville operates on a Prisma Health campus.
  • Furman University and North Greenville University serve the wider area.

Owners of rentals near these campuses and workplaces who tire of managing a tenant can sell as-is for cash instead of preparing the unit for listing.

What is the weather in Greenville and what does it do to a house?

Greenville has a humid subtropical climate. At the Greenville-Spartanburg station the 1991 to 2020 averages run from 42.2 degrees Fahrenheit in January to 79.9 in July, with about 47 inches of rain a year and a few inches of snow.

The record high is 107 degrees, set July 1, 2012, and the record low is minus 6, set January 30, 1966. Freezing weather runs from about November 4 to April 1, which is a growing season of 217 days.

That swing matters for houses. Summer humidity wears on crawl spaces and HVAC systems, and winter freezes can split exposed pipes in vacant homes. If you inherited a house that sat empty through a winter, plumbing is worth checking before any sale.

How do roads, flights and buses get around Greenville?

Interstate 85 runs along the southeast edge of the city, I-185 forms a southern beltway, and I-385 links downtown to I-26. US 25, 29, 123 and 276 also pass through.

Greenville-Spartanburg International Airport, in nearby Greer, handled over 2.56 million passengers in 2023 and ranks third in the state. Greenville Downtown Airport is the busiest general aviation airport in South Carolina. Greenlink buses are run by the city under a 2008 agreement with the county, and Amtrak's Crescent stops in town.

Whether your street is near a bus line, an interchange or downtown is worth mentioning when you describe the house.

Who bills Greenville property tax, and when is it due?

Greenville County sends the property tax bill for homes inside the city. The Tax Collector's office is in the South Building, Suite 1100-S, at 864.467.7050, and bills are due without penalty by January 15.

The county states that the tax on a property follows the property rather than the person, which is why unpaid tax comes out of a sale at closing. If you are unsure how the city's own levy appears on your bill, ask the Tax Collector, since that detail was not on a page we could open.

DatePenalty step
January 163 percent added
February 27 percent more
March 175 percent more, plus $15.00 execution cost

The state schedule is in S.C. Code 12-45-180.

How can a Greenville homeowner challenge a new value?

Send a written objection to Greenville County Real Property Services at Greenville County Square, Suite 1000, phone 864.467.7300. When a notice raises value by $1,000 or more, state law allows 90 days from the mailing date.

  • Include the tax map number, your reasons and what you think the value is.
  • Use mail or hand delivery, because email and fax are not accepted.
  • If no notice came, the default deadline is January 15.

After the county's review you have 30 days to ask the County Board of Assessment Appeals to hear it, and 30 more days from the Board's written decision to reach the Administrative Law Judge Division.

What changes when a Greenville house sells?

A sale normally counts as an assessable transfer of interest, so the county revalues the house to December 31 of the year of the transfer and drops the 15 percent cap on increases. The new owner typically gets a fresh assessment notice the following year.

The January 1 owner of record decides the name on a bill. When a deed changes later in the year, both names appear that year.

The owner-occupied 4 percent rate and the school-tax credit need an original-signature application by January 15, so a landlord who sells a rental to an owner-occupant is handing over a house that can qualify. The reverse is true for a buyer who turns a home into a rental.

The Register of Deeds records the deed at Suite S-2100, Greenville County Square, 301 University Ridge. State and county recording tax together is $1.85 per $500 of value under Title 12, Chapter 24.

What if the tax goes unpaid in Greenville?

After March 17 the county treats the bill as delinquent, issues an execution notice, and can advertise the property for a public tax sale at the Greenville Convention Center. The owner has 12 months after the sale to redeem by paying the taxes, penalties, costs and graduated interest.

The tax deed conveys only the county's interest, not a warranty deed. Selling before the auction avoids that outcome. Exact sale dates change each year, so call 864.467.7050 for the current schedule.

Short-term rental rules are another local topic. We could not open a city page on the current short-term rental regulations, so ask the City of Greenville directly before you plan around that use.

More questions about Greenville, SC Property Tax Guide

Who collects property tax for a house inside Greenville city limits?

Greenville County's Tax Collector sends the bill and takes payment. The office is at 864.467.7050, and tax is due without penalty by January 15.

What happens to my Greenville house tax if I sell in the middle of the year?

The balance follows the property, so the title company pays what is owed from your proceeds. If the deed changes after January 1, both owners' names show on that year's bill.

How long do I have to object to a Greenville assessment?

You have 90 days from the mailing of a notice that raised value by $1,000 or more. With no notice, the usual deadline is January 15, and objections must be written.

Is the Greenville property tax guide the same as the county guide?

They share the same offices, because the county assesses and collects for the city. The city page focuses on the city itself, while the county page covers all of Greenville County.

Can a Greenville house sell if it has already gone to tax sale?

Yes, within 12 months of the sale the owner can redeem. After that, the bidder can receive a tax deed, which is why many owners sell before the auction.

Columbia by the numbers

Where is Columbia, SC and which counties does it cover?

Columbia is near the geographic center of South Carolina, at the fall line where the Broad and Saluda rivers join to form the Congaree. It sits roughly halfway between the Atlantic Ocean and the Blue Ridge Mountains at an elevation of 276 feet.

The city covers 140.68 square miles and lies mostly in Richland County, with portions in Lexington and Kershaw counties. That split matters for a seller, because the county that bills your parcel is the one whose assessor, auditor and treasurer you deal with. This page details Richland County's offices. If your house is on the Lexington or Kershaw side, ask that county's offices for their dates and rules.

What is the history of Columbia?

The General Assembly approved Columbia as the state capital on March 22, 1786, and it became South Carolina's first planned capital. Surveyor John Guignard laid out its grid five years before the plan for Washington, D.C.

Columbia was incorporated as a town in 1805 and chartered as a city in 1854. Union forces captured it on February 17, 1865, and fire destroyed much of it the next day. The University of South Carolina was chartered in 1801 as South Carolina College and now enrolls more than 30,000 students on its Columbia campus.

How many people live in Columbia and who employs them?

The 2020 census counted 136,632 people, making Columbia the second-largest city in South Carolina after Charleston. The 2025 estimate is 147,035, and the six-county metro area had 879,918 residents in 2025.

Government and education anchor the local economy. State agencies, the University of South Carolina and Fort Jackson are among the largest employers, alongside Prisma Health Midlands and BlueCross BlueShield of South Carolina. Headquarters in the city include First Citizens Bank, Colonial Life, AgFirst Farm Credit Bank and SouthState Bank, and manufacturers named include Michelin, Honeywell, Square D, Westinghouse Electric and FN Herstal.

What do Columbia's climate and roads mean for a house?

Columbia has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and generally mild winters. Annual precipitation is about 45 inches and snowfall averages about 1.2 inches. The record high is 113 degrees Fahrenheit, set June 29, 2012, and the record low is minus 2 degrees on February 14, 1899.

Four interstates serve the city.

  • I-20 runs west to east and I-26 runs northwest to southeast.
  • I-77 heads north toward Rock Hill and Charlotte and gives access to Fort Jackson.
  • I-126 links downtown with I-26 and I-20.
  • Columbia Metropolitan Airport has service from American Eagle, Delta Connection and United Express, and Amtrak's Silver Star stops in the city.
  • The COMET agency runs local transit.

Which neighborhoods and school districts serve Columbia?

Wikipedia lists these neighborhoods: Arsenal Hill, Congaree Vista, Cottontown/Bellevue, Elmwood Park, Five Points, Granby Mill Village, Old Shandon, Rosewood, University Hill and Waverly. Cottontown/Bellevue and Waverly are listed as historic districts.

Richland County School District One serves most of the city, and Richland County School District Two serves northern portions as well as secondary students on Fort Jackson. Lexington and Richland County School District Five covers small areas. The Department of Defense Education Activity runs elementary schools on the base.

Who bills Columbia property tax in Richland County?

In Richland County the Assessor assigns a value, the Auditor calculates the tax and prepares bills, and the Treasurer collects and distributes the payment. All three are at 2020 Hampton St., Columbia.

  • Assessor: Suite 2058, phone 803-576-2640.
  • Auditor: Suite 2067, phone 803-576-2600.
  • Treasurer: phone 803-576-2250. Hours are Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Payment options on the county's property tax page are online, in person, by mail, or through a monthly payment plan that you request. The county pages we opened did not list a real property due date, so use the state penalty statute as a guide: 3% is added if tax is unpaid by January 16, another 7% by February 2, and another 5% by March 17 (S.C. Code 12-45-180). Ask the Treasurer for the current bill and payoff.

How can I appeal a Richland County assessment?

File a written objection with the Assessor within 90 days of the dated reassessment notice. With no notice that year, the deadline is the first penalty date on the current year's real property tax bill.

The county offers an online appeal portal, and the Board of Assessment Appeals hears disputes between the Assessor and the taxpayer. A representative needs a power of attorney (Form SC2848), and an entity-owned property needs articles of organization or an operating agreement. State law sets the same 90-day period (S.C. Code 12-60-2510).

The Assessor's address is 2020 Hampton St., Suite 2058, Columbia, SC 29204. The county page did not state its reassessment cycle, so ask the office when the next notices go out.

Why do Columbia rental owners pay more?

Owner-occupied homes are assessed at 4% and all other real property, including rentals and second homes, at 6%. The state sets those ratios, so check which one appears on your bill.

The City of Columbia's 2022 competitive property tax plan went further. It put the effective tax rate on commercial and rental property at 2.92% of value in Richland School District One and 3.55% in District Two. On a $250,000 property, it said annual tax is $7,288 in District One and $8,886 in District Two, and that rentals pay 3.9 times more than owner-occupied property. That was a city planning document and not a tax bill, so check your actual notice.

The 6% rate also applies to a house that has stopped being a primary residence.

What happens with unpaid taxes and the Richland County tax sale?

Unpaid property tax in Richland County can lead to the annual tax sale, typically held in the fall. The 2026 sale was scheduled for Monday, November 2, 2026, with Tuesday, November 3 as a backup day, at Township Auditorium, 1703 Taylor St., Columbia.

An owner could stop a sale by paying everything at the Treasurer's office by 5 p.m. Friday, October 30, 2026, in cash or a certified bank cashier's check only. Personal, company and escrow checks were not accepted. Bids start at the delinquent taxes plus costs and the 2026 taxes, and properties are sold as is, with no warranty.

The county page did not state a redemption period, but state law gives 12 months from the sale (S.C. Code 12-51-90). The county lists delinquenttax@richlandcountysc.gov for tax sale questions, and a payment plan can be requested at plannedpayment@richlandcountysc.gov. If you owe tax and want to sell, you can usually clear the amount from sale proceeds, but ask first about payoff timing.

More questions about Columbia, SC Property Tax Guide

Which county do I pay property tax to if I live in Columbia?

Most Columbia addresses are in Richland County, so you pay the Richland County Treasurer. Parts of the city are in Lexington and Kershaw counties, so check your bill to see which county sent it.

How long do I have to appeal my Richland County assessment?

You have 90 days from the dated reassessment notice to file a written objection with the Assessor. Without a notice, the deadline is the first penalty date on that year's real property tax bill.

Does Richland County offer a property tax payment plan?

Yes. The county's property tax page lets you request a monthly plan, and plannedpayment@richlandcountysc.gov is listed for planned payments. The Delinquent Taxes page says the full amount must be paid to avoid further action.

Can I stop a Richland County tax sale?

Yes, by paying all amounts due before the deadline, which was 5 p.m. on October 30 for the 2026 sale. The Treasurer accepted only cash or a certified bank cashier's check at that stage.

Why is my Columbia rental taxed at 6%?

South Carolina assesses owner-occupied homes at 4% and other real property at 6%. A rental, second home or vacant house does not qualify for the 4% legal residence rate.

Myrtle Beach by the numbers

Where is Myrtle Beach and how big is it?

Myrtle Beach is a resort city in Horry County, in northeastern South Carolina, at the center of the roughly 60-mile Grand Strand. It covers 23.69 square miles, almost all of it land, and sits about 94 miles northeast of Charleston and 74 miles southwest of Wilmington, North Carolina.

The city had 35,682 residents in the 2020 census and an estimate of 40,937 for 2025. The median age in 2020 was 49.4, and 25.4 percent of residents were 65 or older. The Intracoastal Waterway has separated the city from the mainland since 1936.

Because the city is small and the visitor count is large, a house here may be a primary home, a retiree's place or a short-term rental, and the tax treatment differs for each.

How did Myrtle Beach get started?

Myrtle Beach began as a lightly settled coastal stretch that became a resort after a railroad arrived in 1900. The Conway and Seashore Railroad was chartered on February 28, 1899 and began daily service on May 1, 1900, and the Seaside Inn opened in 1901.

The Burroughs and Collins Company bought much of the Withers family land in 1881, and a post office named Withers opened in 1888. The name Myrtle Beach honors the southern wax myrtle shrub. The place was incorporated as a town on March 12, 1938 and as a city in 1957. Kings Highway, now U.S. 17, was paved in 1940.

That timeline explains the housing stock: older cottages near the oceanfront, and much newer condos and subdivisions further in. The median build year for the city's homes was 1992 in the data on our page.

What drives the Myrtle Beach economy?

Tourism dominates the Myrtle Beach economy, supported by hotels, restaurants, golf, attractions and retail. The area reports more than 20 million visitors a year, and the city has roughly 425 hotels and between 1,800 and 1,900 restaurants.

  • The Boardwalk opened in 2010 and the 200-foot SkyWheel in May 2011.
  • The Convention Center opened in 2003.
  • Grand Strand Medical Center has 369 beds, and Horry County Schools has about 40,000 students.
  • Myrtle Beach International Airport, three miles southwest of downtown, sits on the former Air Force base that closed in 1993.

The main roads are U.S. 17, U.S. 501, SC 31 and SC 73, and transit comes from Coast RTA. Many owners here depend on seasonal work or rental income, so the January 15 bill can arrive at a slow point in the year.

What does the coast mean for a Myrtle Beach house?

Myrtle Beach has a humid subtropical climate with about 53.56 inches of precipitation a year, and hurricanes are the main risk. The worst storm in local history was Hurricane Hazel in 1954, and the most recent significant damage came from Hurricane Hugo in 1989.

Direct hits are rare, and weaker tropical storms are more common. Summer highs run 83 to 91 degrees with lows near 70, and September is the wettest month. Salt air, wind-driven rain and flooding are the issues a buyer's inspector will look at first: roof covering, windows, siding, HVAC and crawl-space moisture.

A house with deferred storm repairs can be hard to finance, and that is one reason owners choose a cash sale. Check your insurance and flood status before listing, since the answers affect what buyers can borrow.

Who bills Myrtle Beach property tax, and where do you pay?

The Horry County Treasurer collects real property tax for Myrtle Beach addresses. The county's real property page says notices are mailed to the owner of record, and the city's own news item on its tax calculator says homeowners pay city, county and school district taxes.

The Horry County Treasurer has an office at 332 Hinson Drive in Myrtle Beach, plus offices in Conway, Surfside and Little River:

  • Conway (main): 1301 Second Avenue, Conway, SC 29526
  • Myrtle Beach: 332 Hinson Dr, Myrtle Beach, SC 29579
  • South Strand: 9630 Scipio Lane, Surfside, SC 29588
  • Stephen's Crossroads: 107 Hwy 57 North, Little River, SC 29566

Hours are Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the main number is (843) 915-5470. Payments may be made in person, by mail, in the night deposit box, online, or by phone at 843-428-2126. Card payments carry convenience fees. For exemptions and address changes on real property, the Tax Assessor is at (843) 915-5040, and the Auditor takes homestead questions at (843) 915-5051.

When is Myrtle Beach property tax due, and what are the penalties?

Payment is due in full on or before January 15 of the year after the tax year, and penalties start on January 16, February 2 and March 17 for payments postmarked later. The county says not receiving a bill does not excuse a penalty.

DatePenalty added (S.C. Code 12-45-180)
January 163 percent
February 27 percent more
March 175 percent more, then tax execution

The county's page does not print percentages, so we took them from the statute. Horry County also has an installment payment program, and the treasurer holds an annual public tax sale for delinquent properties. The sale dates were not on the pages we opened, so ask the Treasurer.

Why do second homes and rentals in Myrtle Beach pay more?

A house that is not a legal residence is assessed at 6 percent of fair market value instead of 4 percent. State law also says a home rented more than 72 days a year does not qualify for the 4 percent ratio.

The City of Myrtle Beach published a news item about a tax calculator, maintained by the Myrtle Beach Area Chamber of Commerce at mbtaxcalc.com. It describes a Tourism Development Fee credit for primary homeowners inside the city. In its example, a $200,000 primary residence paid $127.20 in city property taxes after a $504 credit. That example is for owner-occupied homes only, and the page does not give current millage, so ask the county for your actual figures.

For a seller, the difference can be large. An investor selling a vacation rental and an owner selling a primary home face different bills, and a buyer who plans to live in the house must apply for the 4 percent ratio before the first penalty date.

What if you owe tax and want to sell a Myrtle Beach house?

You can sell, and the title company pays the Horry County balance from your proceeds at closing. Get a payoff from the Treasurer first, because penalties change on January 16, February 2 and March 17.

If a tax sale happens first, S.C. Code 12-51-90 lets the owner redeem within twelve months. The interest is 3 percent of the bid in months one to three, 6 in months four to six, 9 in months seven to nine, and 12 in months ten to twelve.

If you disagree with the value, the written objection goes to the assessor within 90 days after the assessment notice is mailed under S.C. Code 12-60-2510. The Horry County pages we opened did not state an appeal deadline of their own, so call the Assessor at (843) 915-5040 for the form.

More questions about Myrtle Beach, SC Property Tax Guide

Who collects property tax in Myrtle Beach?

Horry County does. The Treasurer has an office at 332 Hinson Drive in Myrtle Beach and the main office at 1301 Second Avenue in Conway.

When is Myrtle Beach property tax due?

It is due on or before January 15. Penalties start on January 16, then February 2 and March 17.

Can I pay my Myrtle Beach property tax online?

Yes. Horry County accepts online payment by check or Visa, MasterCard or Discover, and card payments carry convenience fees.

What is the Horry County Assessor's phone number?

It is (843) 915-5040, for exemptions, sold property and real property address changes.

Do rentals in Myrtle Beach get the 4 percent rate?

Not if the home is rented more than 72 days a year. State law then treats it as other real property at 6 percent.

Can I sell a Myrtle Beach house with back taxes owed?

Yes. The balance is paid from the proceeds at closing, as long as the price covers it. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure.
